title: Stereotactic radiosurgery and fractionated radiotherapy for multiple brain metastases. A prospective multicentre single-arm trial.
summary:
Brain metastases are very common and can lead to serious neurological symptoms. As systemic therapy for metastatic tumor patients continues to improve, there are now some long-term survivors with brain metastases. Therefore, the therapy of brain metastases is becoming increasingly important. Whole-brain radiation is the standard therapy for patients with multiple brain metastases. In patients with 1-3 brain metastases, the standard therapy is radiosurgery or microsurgery. For better local control, adjuvant radiotherapy should be performed after resection. To date, adjuvant whole-brain radiation has been used to improve local control. A large randomized European multicenter study showed that whole brain irradiation after local treatment of 1-3 brain metastases (radiosurgery or resection) could reduce the rate of distant cerebral brain metastases. However, this could not increase survival and leads to neurocognitive deficits as a side effect.
Even in patients with multiple brain metastases, whole-brain irradiation is currently the subject of much controversy. In a Japanese study, patients with multiple brain metastases were treated radiosurgically with up to 10 brain metastases. Whole-brain radiation was not used. The survival of the patient groups with 2-4 brain metastases and in the group with 5-10 brain metastases was the same. As a result of this study, there are more and more radiation therapy centers that do not perform whole-brain radiation in the case of multiple brain metastases and carry out local radiation therapy in the form of radiosurgery. In addition, there are more and more patients who, despite multiple brain metastases, refuse whole-brain radiation for fear of neurocognitive deficits.
Other studies (HIPPORAD) are currently investigating whole-brain irradiation with hippocampal protection, since it can be assumed that episodic memory deficits in particular are associated with damage to the hippocampus after irradiation. A phase III study on hippocampal sparing has already shown that memory and quality of life could be preserved compared to patients with conventional whole-brain radiation (Brown et al., 2020).
Other side effects such as leukoencephalopathy and cerebral atrophy can also occur after whole-brain irradiation, which is why dose de-escalation to the whole brain was already carried out in the HIPPORAD study.
By omitting whole-brain radiation, we assume that the cognitive performance of the patients will improve or remain constant 3 months after treatment. In the case of rapid cerebral progression, further radiosurgery or whole-brain irradiation can be carried out as salvage therapy.
conditions: Secondary malignant neoplasm of brain and cerebral meninges

interventions.name: Stereotactic radiosurgery or stereotactic fractionated radiotherapy of multiple (4-10) brain metastases

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1.	Patient's written informed consent has been obtained
2.	Age 18-80 years, male or female
3.	Legal capacity, patient is able to understand the nature, significance, and consequences of the trial
4.	At least 4 brain metastases of solid tumours, with at least one and not exceeding 10 metastases ≥ 3 mm (i.e. eligible for SRS/SFRT)
5.	RPA classification I or II
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Simultaneous participation in other interventional trials which could interfere with this trial 
2.	Participation in an interventional clinical trial within the last thirty days before the start of this trial, previous participation in this trial
3.	Known or persistent abuse of medication, drugs or alcohol
4.	Persons who are in a relationship of dependence/employment with the sponsor or the investigator
5.	Pregnancy, nursing or patient not willing to prevent a pregnancy during treatment
6.	Cerebral lymphomas, metastases of germ cell tumours, small cell lung carcinoma
7.	Metastases (either preirradiated or not) or resection cavity within the hippocampus or in a distance of 7 mm to the hippocampus
8.	Acute neurological symptoms demanding an immediate start of RT
9.	CNS diseases or syndromes accompanied by cognitive deficits or radiological changes of the brain, e.g., dementia, major depression, clinically manifest hypertensive encephalopathy, meningiosis carcinomatosa
10.	Previous brain irradiation (SRS/SFRT) of >1 brain metastasis >3cm or >3 brain metastases >1cm each
11.	Previous brain irradiation <3 months before start of treatment
12.	Previous surgical resection (± adjuvant SFRT) of >1 brain metastasis (biopsy allowed)
13.	Previous surgical resection of 1 brain metastasis <4 weeks before start of treatment
14.	Uncontrolled pretreated brain metastasis/-es after SRS/SFRT
15.	RT planning conforming to constraints for organs at risk not feasible (including previous cranial irradiation)
16.	Benzodiazepines, barbiturates, topiramate, hydantoine as antiepileptic medication
17.	> 1 brainstem metastasis ≥3mm
18.	Brainstem metastasis >2cm
19.	Brain metastasis >3.5cm
20.	Resection cavity eligible for dose escalation >3.5cm
